answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, any delivery-risk increase is unacceptable, ruling out switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor despite cost pressure (memory_c2 shows it missed SLA in 3 of 4 quarters). Deferring is also unattractive because the contract expires in 14 days and does not auto-renew, and this line is not flagged as non-critical (unlike memory_c5's case). The strongest precedent for meeting a cost mandate without disrupting a tight supply chain is memory_c4 (renegotiating at renewal recovered margin via benchmarking) combined with memory_c6 (multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service). Negotiating terms with the incumbent before the 14-day expiry lets us pursue part of the 18% spend cut while preserving continuity and avoiding onboarding/integration risk during a no-buffer period. I verified c4 and c2 because they most directly bear on whether renegotiation reliably yields savings and on the concrete risk profile of the tempting low-cost alternative.
